https://www.dw.com/en/canada-fire-at-mil.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ON8t Officials have warned of 'overwhelmed' hospitals Image: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday said that the fire at a military base in Alberta was one of the worst tragedies the army has suffered in peace time. "It is with deep sadness that I can confirm, at this time, that four service members have lost their lives and that their loved ones have been notified," Carney said in the capital Ottawa, adding that "dozens of others have been seriously injured." "We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery," Carney said. "And we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss, they will not carry it alone because in Canada we take care of one another." Defense Minister David McGuinty had earlier confirmed "fatalities and injuries" as a result of the incident on the base, adding that there would be "more to say in the coming hours and days." The cause of the fire still remains unknown, with Canadian authorities saying the situation continues to evolve. Medical facilities around base 'overwhelmed' A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, which is located some 180 kilometers (120 miles) northwest of the base, told national broadcaster CBC that people were being brought to hospitals across the city. Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, said health-care facilities around the base itself had been "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people requiring medical aid. "This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," he said. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster." The injured were brought to Wainwright Health Center Image: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta? The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was spreading rapidly due to high winds. "The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed ... Emergency crews remain focused on protecting life safety, homes, and other structures," it said. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected. "We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media. The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada . Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief PRAGUE/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš faced mounting pressure Wednesday after thousands of demonstrators rallied in central Prague against government plans to overhaul public broadcasting, amid warnings that the changes could threaten press freedom in the European Union nation. The crowds appeared to number in the tens of thousands, according to an estimate based on aerial imagery reviewed by Worthy News, although no official attendance figure was immediately available. These protests followed an unprecedented one-day strike Tuesday by employees of Czech Television and Czech Radio, who accuse the government of seeking greater political influence over public broadcasters by replacing independent license-fee funding with direct financing from the state budget. Crowds gathered in Prague’s historic Wenceslas Square, where television and radio employees were joined by university students, artists and other supporters demanding that the government withdraw the proposed legislation. BROADCASTERS GO ON STRIKE Protests also occurred in other Czech cities, including Brno and Ostrava, reflecting growing opposition to plans that critics say could weaken two of the country’s most influential news organizations. The industrial action disrupted television and radio programming, with Czech Television’s 24-hour news channel showing a darkened newsroom and presenters dressed in black. Regular broadcasts were replaced in part by archived programs and shortened news bulletins, while radio stations reduced live programming and aired music and previously recorded material. Under the government’s original proposal, existing broadcasting fees paid by households and businesses would be abolished, with Czech Television and Czech Radio instead receiving financing directly from the state budget. BROADCASTING FUNDING AT STAKE Czech households currently pay 205 crowns (about $10) monthly for public television and radio, or roughly $115 annually. The proposed changes would reduce the broadcasters’ combined annual funding by approximately 15 percent, or 1.4 billion crowns ($66 million), to about 7.8 billion crowns ($370 million), according to European media organizations. Critics warn that the cuts could force layoffs, reductions in news coverage and the cancellation of programs. Babiš, a billionaire businessman who returned to power leading a coalition with the Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party and the Motorists, insists the reforms are intended to reduce financial burdens on households and businesses. His government denies seeking to interfere with editorial decisions and argues that public broadcasting can be financed through alternative arrangements without compromising journalistic independence. GOVERNMENT DENIES POLITICAL MOTIVES Babiš has also floated a revised proposal under which broadcasting fees would become voluntary, with guaranteed funding for the broadcasters potentially coming from outside the state budget. Details of that arrangement remain unclear. Journalists and opposition politicians fear that greater government control over funding decisions could expose broadcasters to political pressure and undermine their ability to scrutinize those in power. “Such a funding model opens the door to political pressure and threatens editorial independence,” the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and other media organizations warned in a joint statement. Opponents have drawn parallels with neighboring Hungary and Slovakia, where governments have faced criticism over changes affecting public broadcasting and media independence. MEDIA INDEPENDENCE WARNINGS Hungary’s former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, an ally of Babiš, was repeatedly accused by European institutions and press freedom organizations of weakening independent journalism during his 16 years in power before losing office in April. In Slovakia, Prime Minister Robert Fico’s government has also faced criticism over changes to public broadcasting that opponents argue have increased political influence. The European Commission is assessing the Czech authorities’ response to concerns about the proposed changes, although it has not concluded that the legislation violates European Union rules. The legislation passed an initial parliamentary vote in October but remains subject to further debate, with Babiš indicating that amendments could still be considered. The changes are no longer expected to take effect in January 2027. MORE PROTESTS PLANNED University students are preparing another demonstration for November 10, while the civic movement Million Moments for Democracy has announced a larger rally for November 15 at Prague’s Letná Park. The planned gathering comes shortly before the anniversary of the November 17, 1989, student demonstrations that helped trigger Czechoslovakia’s Velvet Revolution and the collapse of communist rule. The dispute has become a test of the Czech government’s commitment to independent journalism, with protesters warning that the future of public broadcasting could depend on decisions taken in the coming weeks.
